---
title: "Is there a better way to look at the same numbers?"
subtitle: "You will turn a ruler through a cloud of points by hand, then teach it to a computer. All you need is arithmetic."
engine: knitr
---

Here are 30 people. Each dot is one person, placed by two numbers: their height, and their arm span (fingertip to fingertip, arms stretched out). Both are in centimetres.

Look at the shape. Tall people have long arms, short people have short arms. The two numbers rise and fall together, so in a sense they are saying one thing twice. Sometimes the measurements you are handed are an awkward way to look at the data. This lesson is about finding a better way.

## If you could keep only one number per person, which would you keep?

Suppose you had room for one number per person, not two. You want to keep as much as you can of what tells these people apart.

::: {.ask data-veil="true"}
Which one number would you keep?

- **Their height.** A fair choice: it is a real measurement and easy to explain. Press *keep across* and see how much it keeps.
- **Their arm span.** Also fair. Press *keep up* and compare it with height.
- **Something in between.** Good instinct. The dots lie along a slant, not along either edge. Press *keep a slanted one*.
:::

::: {.ink-figure data-figure="reshape-ruler" data-step="0" data-caption="Fig. 1 · 30 made-up people: height across, arm span up"}
:::

Each button lays a ruler through the middle of the cloud. Every dot drops a thread straight onto the ruler, meeting it at a right angle, and the spot where it lands is that person's one number. Try all three.

To judge a choice you need a way to say how spread out the landing spots are. Use the one that goes with the average: the **spread** is the average of the squared distances from the middle. By hand, with four spots at −3, −1, 1 and 3 (the middle is 0): 9 + 1 + 1 + 9 = 20, and 20 divided by 4 is **5**.

Keeping height keeps 42.8% of the spread. Keeping arm span keeps 57.2%. The slanted ruler keeps 92.9%. So the rule for this lesson: **the best single number is the one whose ruler spreads the dots out the most.** Spread is what tells people apart. If every landing spot were in the same place, the one number would tell you nothing.

## What about a slanted ruler at any angle?

The slanted ruler in Fig. 1 sat at 45 degrees, half way between across and up. Nothing says that is the best slant.

::: {.ink-figure data-figure="reshape-ruler" data-step="1" data-caption="Fig. 2 · turn the ruler; the curve fills in wherever you have been · made-up data"}
:::

Drag the ring at the end of the ruler, or the slider, and watch two things: the threads, and the spread in the side column. When the ruler lies along the cloud, the threads are short and the landings are spread far apart. Turn it across the cloud and the landings bunch up in the middle.

The small chart fills in as you explore: the spread at every angle you have visited. Press *try every angle* to sweep the ruler all the way round. It comes to rest at the top of the curve, at 50 degrees: a little better than 45. Leave it wherever you like before you move on: the code below will start from your angle.

### Where does a dot land?

Before any code, work one landing by hand. Put a dot at 3 across and 4 up from the middle. Take a ruler that, for every 1 you go along it, goes 0.6 across and 0.8 up. (It really is 1 long: 0.6 × 0.6 + 0.8 × 0.8 = 0.36 + 0.64 = 1.)

The landing spot is the dot's across times the ruler's across, plus the dot's up times the ruler's up: 3 × 0.6 + 4 × 0.8 = 1.8 + 3.2 = **5**. The dot lands 5 along the ruler. That makes sense: this dot sits exactly on the ruler, 5 from the middle, so its thread has no length at all.

::: {.ask}
You are about to teach this to a computer. How would you know the code is right?

- **Run it on the 30 people and look at the picture.** The picture would look plausible whether the arithmetic was right or slightly off. You could not tell.
- **Give it the dot and the ruler I just did by hand.** Yes. You know the answer is 5. If the code prints anything else, it is wrong, and you know straight away.
:::

### Now tell a computer

First, one tidy-up. The ruler turns about the middle of the cloud, so measure every dot from the middle: take the average height away from each height, and the average arm span away from each arm span. The averages here are 172 cm and 173 cm, so a person 169 cm tall with a 171 cm arm span becomes (−3, −2): 3 cm shorter than average, and 2 cm less arm span.

The cell below fetches the same 30 people you saw in Fig. 1, and the angle you left the ruler at. Fill in the blank and press **Run**. The first run takes a few seconds while Python starts.

::: {.py-cell data-draw="py-plot"}
```python
from page import points, my_angle      # the 30 people in Fig. 1, and your angle from Fig. 2

def centre(pairs):
    n = len(pairs)                                  # how many pairs there are
    avg_across = sum(p[0] for p in pairs) / n       # add up the first numbers, divide
    avg_up = sum(p[1] for p in pairs) / n           # add up the second numbers, divide
    return [(p[0] - avg_across, ____) for p in pairs]

centred = centre(points)
print("First person:", points[0], "becomes", centred[0])

picture = {"points": centred, "hlines": [0], "vlines": [0], "xlim": (-30, 30), "ylim": (-30, 30),
           "xlabel": "height - average", "ylabel": "arm span - average"}
```
::: {.py-solution}
```python
from page import points, my_angle      # the 30 people in Fig. 1, and your angle from Fig. 2

def centre(pairs):
    n = len(pairs)                                  # how many pairs there are
    avg_across = sum(p[0] for p in pairs) / n       # add up the first numbers, divide
    avg_up = sum(p[1] for p in pairs) / n           # add up the second numbers, divide
    return [(p[0] - avg_across, p[1] - avg_up) for p in pairs]

centred = centre(points)
print("First person:", points[0], "becomes", centred[0])

picture = {"points": centred, "hlines": [0], "vlines": [0], "xlim": (-30, 30), "ylim": (-30, 30),
           "xlabel": "height - average", "ylabel": "arm span - average"}
```
:::
:::

A few Python words. `def` gives a set of steps a name, and `return` hands back the answer. `p[0]` is the first number of a pair and `p[1]` the second. The square brackets with a `for` inside build a new list, one entry for every pair. The picture is the same cloud, slid so that the middle sits where the two lines cross.

Now the landing spot, and the ruler. `import math` brings in a toolbox with `sin` and `cos`: for a ruler at a given angle, they say how far across and how far up it points.

::: {.py-cell data-draw="py-plot"}
```python
import math

def land(p, ruler):
    return p[0] * ruler[0] + ____         # across times the ruler's across, plus up times the ruler's up

print(land((3, 4), (0.6, 0.8)))           # by hand this was 5

def ruler_at(angle):
    a = math.radians(angle)               # sin and cos want the angle in their own unit, not degrees
    return (math.cos(a), math.sin(a))     # how far across, and how far up, a ruler at this angle points

r = ruler_at(53.13)
print("A ruler at 53.13 degrees points", round(r[0], 2), "across and", round(r[1], 2), "up")

# only for drawing: the cloud, your ruler, and a thread from every point to where it lands
def ruler_picture(pairs, angle):
    r = ruler_at(angle)
    reach = 0
    threads = []
    for p in pairs:
        reach = max(reach, math.sqrt(p[0] * p[0] + p[1] * p[1]))   # the furthest any point is from the middle
        s = land(p, r)
        threads.append((p, (s * r[0], s * r[1])))        # from the point to its landing spot
    return {"points": pairs, "segments": threads,
            "accent": [(-reach * r[0], -reach * r[1]), (reach * r[0], reach * r[1])],
            "xlim": (-1.1 * reach, 1.1 * reach), "ylim": (-1.1 * reach, 1.1 * reach),
            "notes": ["angle " + str(angle)]}

picture = ruler_picture(centred, my_angle)
```
::: {.py-solution}

def land(p, ruler):
    return p[0] * ruler[0] + p[1] * ruler[1]     # across times the ruler's across, plus up times the ruler's up

print(land((3, 4), (0.6, 0.8)))           # by hand this was 5

def ruler_at(angle):
    a = math.radians(angle)               # sin and cos want the angle in their own unit, not degrees
    return (math.cos(a), math.sin(a))     # how far across, and how far up, a ruler at this angle points

r = ruler_at(53.13)
print("A ruler at 53.13 degrees points", round(r[0], 2), "across and", round(r[1], 2), "up")

# only for drawing: the cloud, your ruler, and a thread from every point to where it lands
def ruler_picture(pairs, angle):
    r = ruler_at(angle)
    reach = 0
    threads = []
    for p in pairs:
        reach = max(reach, math.sqrt(p[0] * p[0] + p[1] * p[1]))   # the furthest any point is from the middle
        s = land(p, r)
        threads.append((p, (s * r[0], s * r[1])))        # from the point to its landing spot
    return {"points": pairs, "segments": threads,
            "accent": [(-reach * r[0], -reach * r[1]), (reach * r[0], reach * r[1])],
            "xlim": (-1.1 * reach, 1.1 * reach), "ylim": (-1.1 * reach, 1.1 * reach),

:::

It should print 5.0, the answer you got by hand. The second line is a check on `ruler_at`: the ruler from the hand example, 0.6 across and 0.8 up, is the one at about 53 degrees. The picture under the cell is your ruler from Fig. 2, with every thread, drawn from the code's own numbers.

## Which angle spreads them out the most?

By hand you turned the ruler and watched a number. The computer will do the same, one degree at a time, and remember the best angle so far. `for angle in range(180)` repeats the indented lines with `angle` set to 0, then 1, then 2, up to 179. (At 180 degrees the ruler is back where it started, pointing the other way.) `if` runs its lines only when the test is true.

::: {.py-cell data-draw="py-plot"}
```python
def spread(values):
    total = 0
    for v in values:
        total = total + v * v                # the middle is 0, so v is the distance from it
    return total / len(values)

def best_ruler(pairs):
    best_angle = 0
    best_spread = 0
    for angle in range(180):                 # 0, 1, 2, ... up to 179 degrees
        s = spread([land(p, ruler_at(angle)) for p in pairs])
        if s > best_spread:
            best_spread = s
            best_angle = ____                # a bigger spread: which angle should it remember?
    return best_angle, best_spread

mine = spread([land(p, ruler_at(my_angle)) for p in centred])
best_angle, best_spread = best_ruler(centred)
total = spread([p[0] for p in centred]) + spread([p[1] for p in centred])

print("Your angle:", my_angle, "  spread", round(mine, 1))
print("Best angle:", best_angle, "  spread", round(best_spread, 1), "of", round(total, 1))

frames = [ruler_picture(centred, a) for a in range(0, 180, 6)]    # the ruler at every 6th angle
frames.append(ruler_picture(centred, best_angle))                  # and at the best one
```
::: {.py-solution}
```python
def spread(values):
    total = 0
    for v in values:
        total = total + v * v                # the middle is 0, so v is the distance from it
    return total / len(values)

def best_ruler(pairs):
    best_angle = 0
    best_spread = 0
    for angle in range(180):                 # 0, 1, 2, ... up to 179 degrees
        s = spread([land(p, ruler_at(angle)) for p in pairs])
        if s > best_spread:
            best_spread = s
            best_angle = angle               # a bigger spread: remember this angle
    return best_angle, best_spread

mine = spread([land(p, ruler_at(my_angle)) for p in centred])
best_angle, best_spread = best_ruler(centred)
total = spread([p[0] for p in centred]) + spread([p[1] for p in centred])

print("Your angle:", my_angle, "  spread", round(mine, 1))
print("Best angle:", best_angle, "  spread", round(best_spread, 1), "of", round(total, 1))

frames = [ruler_picture(centred, a) for a in range(0, 180, 6)]    # the ruler at every 6th angle
frames.append(ruler_picture(centred, best_angle))                  # and at the best one
```
:::
:::

`best_ruler` hands back two answers at once, and `best_angle, best_spread = best_ruler(centred)` catches them in two names. Watch the margin while it runs: the lines inside the loop run 180 times. The picture then turns the ruler round and lets it settle on the best angle. Compare what it prints with Fig. 2 after *try every angle*: the best angle is 50 degrees, with a spread of 132.1 out of 141.3. Same dots, same rule, same answer.

`total` is the spread across plus the spread up: everything there is to keep. Your own angle's spread is printed beside the best, so you can see how close your hand got.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="The same thing in symbols"}
Write a centred point as $(x_i, y_i)$ and a ruler at angle $\theta$ as $(\cos\theta, \sin\theta)$. The landing spot of point $i$ is

$$t_i = x_i \cos\theta + y_i \sin\theta$$

and the spread along the ruler is

$$\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} t_i^2$$

Read the big Σ as "add these up, for every point from 1 to $n$". The best ruler is the $\theta$ that makes this as large as possible.
:::

## What did you lose?

The best ruler keeps 93.5% of the spread. The other 6.5% has not vanished: it lies across the ruler, in the threads.

::: {.ink-figure data-figure="reshape-ruler" data-step="2" data-caption="Fig. 3 · the best ruler, the one at a right angle to it, and every person collapsed onto the first · made-up data"}
:::

The thin line crosses the best ruler at a right angle. Measure the spread along it and you get 9.2. Add the two: 132.1 + 9.2 = 141.3, exactly the total. That is no accident. Any two rulers at a right angle split the total spread between them, the same way 3 × 3 + 4 × 4 makes 5 × 5. The best ruler takes as much of it as it can, and the one at a right angle holds whatever is left.

Press *keep one number*. Every person slides along their thread onto the best ruler. Two numbers per person have become one, and the short threads you watched disappear are all that was lost.

::: {.py-cell data-draw="py-plot"}
```python
first = ruler_at(best_angle)
second = ruler_at(best_angle + 90)               # at a right angle to the first
s1 = spread([land(p, first) for p in centred])
s2 = spread([land(p, second) for p in centred])

print("Along the best ruler:", round(s1, 1))
print("At a right angle:    ", round(s2, 1))
print("Together:            ", round(s1 + s2, 1), "  the total was", round(total, 1))
print("Share kept:", round(100 * s1 / ____, 1), "%")

frames = []
for step in range(9):                            # slide every point a little further onto the ruler
    t = step / 8                                 # 0 at the start, 1 when it has landed
    moved = []
    for p in centred:
        s = land(p, first)
        moved.append((p[0] + t * (s * first[0] - p[0]), p[1] + t * (s * first[1] - p[1])))
    frames.append({"points": moved, "xlim": (-30, 30), "ylim": (-30, 30),
                   "accent": [(-27 * first[0], -27 * first[1]), (27 * first[0], 27 * first[1])],
                   "lines": [[(-27 * second[0], -27 * second[1]), (27 * second[0], 27 * second[1])]]})
```

`append` adds one more entry to the end of a list. The picture plays the collapse that Fig. 3 showed, worked out by your code: 9 small slides, each a little closer to the ruler.

With two measurements, going from two numbers to one is a small saving. With fifty measurements that mostly rise and fall together, a handful of rulers can keep nearly all of the spread. You find them the same way: the first ruler takes the most, the next one, at a right angle to it, takes the most of what is left, and so on until you have kept enough.

## How does it break?

Nothing so far cared what units the measurements were in, because both were centimetres. Suppose the height had been written down in metres instead: 1.69 rather than 169. Same people, same tape measure. Run it.

::: {.py-cell data-draw="py-plot" data-aside="true"}
```python
mixed = centre([(p[0] / 100, p[1]) for p in points])    # height in metres, arm span still in cm

print("First person in cm:", centred[0])
print("Height in metres:  ", (round(mixed[0][0], 2), mixed[0][1]))
print("Best angle, all in cm:        ", best_ruler(centred)[0])
print("Best angle, height in metres: ", best_ruler(mixed)[0])

picture = ruler_picture(mixed, best_ruler(mixed)[0])
```
:::

`best_ruler(...)[0]` takes the first of the two answers it hands back, the angle. In metres, every height is within 0.2 of the middle, while arm spans still wander by many centimetres. So the best ruler points almost straight up: it keeps arm span and ignores height. The data did not change. Only the way one number was written down. The picture shows it: drawn on the same scale both ways, the heights have squashed into a thin column.

::: {.ask}
What would you do about it?

- **Make sure both are in the same units.** That works here. It does not work for age in years and income in dollars, which can never share a unit.
- **Scale each measurement first.** Yes. Divide each centred measurement by its own typical distance from the middle. Then a "1" means "one typical step" for every measurement, whatever its units.
- **Leave out the measurement with small numbers.** That is what the ruler just did, without being asked. It is the problem, not the cure.
:::

The typical distance from the middle is the square root of the spread (`math.sqrt`: the number that, times itself, gives the one you started with). You met this tidy-up as scaling.

::: {.py-cell data-draw="py-plot"}
```python
def scaled(pairs):
    across = math.sqrt(spread([p[0] for p in pairs]))    # typical distance from the middle, across
    up = math.sqrt(spread([p[1] for p in pairs]))        # and up
    return [(p[0] / across, p[1] / ____) for p in pairs]

mixed = centre([(p[0] / 100, p[1]) for p in points])    # the same people, height in metres

print("Scaled, starting from cm:    ", best_ruler(scaled(centred))[0])
print("Scaled, starting from metres:", best_ruler(scaled(mixed))[0])

picture = ruler_picture(scaled(mixed), best_ruler(scaled(mixed))[0])
```
::: {.py-solution}
```python
def scaled(pairs):
    across = math.sqrt(spread([p[0] for p in pairs]))    # typical distance from the middle, across
    up = math.sqrt(spread([p[1] for p in pairs]))        # and up
    return [(p[0] / across, p[1] / up) for p in pairs]

mixed = centre([(p[0] / 100, p[1]) for p in points])    # the same people, height in metres

print("Scaled, starting from cm:    ", best_ruler(scaled(centred))[0])
print("Scaled, starting from metres:", best_ruler(scaled(mixed))[0])

picture = ruler_picture(scaled(mixed), best_ruler(scaled(mixed))[0])
```
:::
:::

After scaling, metres and centimetres give the same answer, and the cloud has its slant back. The angle is 45 degrees rather than 50, because now each measurement counts equally instead of in centimetres.

### What the ruler does not know

Two more limits, and neither is a bug.

The ruler is chosen for spread, nothing else. It never asks whether the new number is useful for predicting anything. Sometimes the most spread-out direction is also the useful one. Sometimes it is mostly noise, and the thing you care about hides in a direction with very little spread, which a ruler chosen for spread would throw away. If you plan to predict with the new numbers, test the predictions, as in the lesson on unseen data.

Each new number is a blend. The best ruler points 0.64 across and 0.77 up, so every landing is a bit of height plus a bit of arm span. You cannot read it as "height matters most" or "arm span matters most". The ruler turned the picture. It did not rank your measurements.

## What about a lopsided measurement?

A different awkward measurement. Here are 60 made-up waiting times at a clinic, in minutes. Most people wait a few minutes. A few wait half an hour or more. Piled up, they make a heap on the left and a long thin tail on the right.

The average gets dragged out by the tail: 41 of the 60 waits are below it. A pile that was balanced would have about half on each side.

::: {.ask data-veil="true"}
How could you pull that tail in without throwing anyone out?

- **Leave out the long waits.** They are real people who really waited. Removing them changes the facts, not the way you look at them.
- **Subtract something from every wait.** That slides the whole pile along. The tail is just as long as before.
- **Squeeze the big numbers more than the small ones.** Yes. A stretch that pulls 50 in a lot and 2 in a little brings the tail back toward the heap.
:::

::: {.ink-figure data-figure="boxcox-figure" data-step="0" data-caption="Fig. 4 · 60 made-up waiting times, and a stretch you control"}
:::

Drag the average line toward the middle of the pile, or slide the strength, and watch the pile even out. Or press *take the logarithm*. The numbers under the axis stay in minutes, so you can see what is happening: 2, 5, 10, 20 and 50 start far apart at the right and get pulled together.

The **logarithm** counts how many times you multiply by 10 to get there. 10 is one ten, so its logarithm is 1. 100 is 10 × 10, so its logarithm is 2. And 1 needs no tens at all, so its logarithm is 0. A number between 10 and 100, such as 20, lands between 1 and 2 (about 1.3). So the logarithm turns "times 10" into "plus 1": the gap from 5 to 50 becomes the same size as the gap from 0.5 to 5. Long waits get pulled in hard, short ones hardly at all.

At the log, the lopsidedness number in the side column is close to 0 and 32 of the 60 waits sit below the average: nearly half. Slide past it and the pile tips the other way. The stretch can be overdone.

::: {.py-cell data-draw="py-plot"}
```python
from page import waits                         # the 60 waiting times in Fig. 4, in minutes

print(math.log10(10), math.log10(100), math.log10(1))     # 1, 2 and 0, as worked by hand

logs = [math.log10(w) for w in waits]

def below_average(values):
    avg = sum(values) / len(values)
    count = 0
    for v in values:
        if v < avg:
            count = count + 1
    return count

print("In minutes:", below_average(waits), "of 60 below the average")
print("After log: ", below_average(____), "of 60 below the average")

bars = []
for i in range(18):                            # boxes 0 to 0.1, 0.1 to 0.2, ... up to 1.8
    low = i / 10
    count = 0
    for v in logs:
        if low <= v < low + 0.1:
            count = count + 1
    bars.append((low + 0.05, count))
picture = {"bars": bars, "vlines": [sum(logs) / len(logs)],
           "xlabel": "logarithm of minutes", "ylabel": "how many"}
```
::: {.py-solution}
```python
from page import waits                         # the 60 waiting times in Fig. 4, in minutes

print(math.log10(10), math.log10(100), math.log10(1))     # 1, 2 and 0, as worked by hand

logs = [math.log10(w) for w in waits]

def below_average(values):
    avg = sum(values) / len(values)
    count = 0
    for v in values:
        if v < avg:
            count = count + 1
    return count

print("In minutes:", below_average(waits), "of 60 below the average")
print("After log: ", below_average(logs), "of 60 below the average")

bars = []
for i in range(18):                            # boxes 0 to 0.1, 0.1 to 0.2, ... up to 1.8
    low = i / 10
    count = 0
    for v in logs:
        if low <= v < low + 0.1:
            count = count + 1
    bars.append((low + 0.05, count))
picture = {"bars": bars, "vlines": [sum(logs) / len(logs)],
           "xlabel": "logarithm of minutes", "ylabel": "how many"}
```
:::
:::

The counts should match Fig. 4 at the log: 41 below the average before, 32 after. The pile under the cell is the stretched waits, boxed in tenths, with the average drawn through it. The figure uses a different logarithm (one built on 2.718 rather than 10), but any logarithm gives the same shape, only a different scale along the bottom.

Why bother? When you fit a line to a lopsided measurement, the misses are usually small where the values are small and large where they are big. Plotted, the misses fan out like a funnel. Methods that fit lines work best when the misses are about the same size everywhere, and the stretch often closes the funnel. It only works on numbers above zero: there is no logarithm of 0 or of a negative number.

A related tidy-up, for measurements taken over time. If two things both drift steadily upward month by month, such as ice cream sales and drownings over a warming year, they will rise together even if neither has anything to do with the other. Fit a straight line to each against time, take it away, and compare what is left. Once the shared drift is gone, the false link usually goes with it.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="The same thing in symbols"}
The stretch in Fig. 4 slides through a family of powers. With $y$ the original value and $\lambda$ (read "lambda") the power,

$$T(y) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{y^{\lambda} - 1}{\lambda} & \text{if } \lambda \neq 0 \\[6pt] \log(y) & \text{if } \lambda = 0 \end{cases}$$

The slider's strength is $1 - \lambda$. A few powers have names:

| $\lambda$ | Stretch | Effect |
|:---------:|:--------|:-------|
| 1 | $y$ (no change) | none |
| 0.5 | $\sqrt{y}$ | mild pull on the large values |
| 0 | $\log(y)$ | strong pull, the most common choice |
| −1 | $1/y$ | very strong |

At $\lambda = 0$ the top line would divide by zero, so the logarithm takes its place. Taking out a drift over time is

$$y_{\text{without drift}} = y - (a_0 + a_1 \cdot \text{time})$$

where $a_0 + a_1 \cdot \text{time}$ is the straight line fitted to $y$ against time.
:::

## What you just built

Everything you did has a name:

| What you did | What it is called |
|:--|:--|
| Measuring every dot from the middle | Centring |
| The spread: average squared distance from the middle | Variance |
| The slanted ruler that keeps the most spread | The first principal component (PC1) |
| The ruler at a right angle to it | The second principal component (PC2) |
| How far across and how far up the ruler points | The loadings, or an eigenvector |
| The spread along the best ruler | The first eigenvalue |
| Where a dot lands on the ruler | Its score, or projection |
| The share of the spread kept | Proportion of variance explained |
| Keeping one number instead of two | Principal component analysis (PCA), a kind of dimension reduction |
| Dividing by the typical distance from the middle | Standardising (z-scores) |
| Stretching a lopsided measurement | A transformation: the log, or the Box-Cox family of powers |
| The lopsidedness number | Skewness |
| Taking a steady drift out of a series | Detrending |

A library does not try 180 angles. For two or for fifty measurements, it finds every ruler at once with some linear algebra: the rulers are the eigenvectors of a table of how each pair of measurements varies together, and the spreads along them are the eigenvalues. You decide how many to keep by plotting the spread each one holds and looking for where the drop flattens (a scree plot), or by keeping rulers until they hold 80 to 90% of the total. Measurements that move together cause trouble for a fitted line, because the line cannot tell which one deserves the credit. Rulers at right angles do not move together, which is why PCA is often run before fitting. It only saves anything when some measurements move together; if none do, the best rulers are just your original measurements again. And it needs measurements that are numbers on a scale, not categories. Box-Cox, likewise, tries many powers and picks the one that leaves the misses most balanced.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Reference: the same ideas in R"}
Every plot below is produced by the R on this page. Open "The R" under any of them to see the code.

Two features that carry overlapping information.

```{r}
#| label: plot-correlated-data
#| fig-cap: "These two features are highly correlated — they carry redundant information"

library(ggplot2)
set.seed(42)

n <- 100

# Two correlated features
x1 <- rnorm(n, 50, 10)
x2 <- 0.8 * x1 + rnorm(n, 10, 5)  # correlated with x1

df <- data.frame(x1 = x1, x2 = x2)

ggplot(df, aes(x1, x2)) +
  geom_point(size = 2, color = "gray40") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  labs(x = "Feature 1 (e.g., assessment score)",
       y = "Feature 2 (e.g., homework score)",
       title = paste0("Correlation = ", round(cor(x1, x2), 2),
                       " — these carry overlapping information"))
```

The same data standardised, with the PCA directions drawn on it, and then in the rotated space. PC1 (horizontal) holds the main spread, PC2 (vertical) holds what is left, and the two are uncorrelated.

```{r}
#| label: plot-pca-rotation
#| fig-cap: "PCA rotates the axes to align with the directions of maximum variance"

# Standardize
df_s <- scale(df)

# PCA
pca <- prcomp(df_s)

# Plot original data with PCA directions
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))

# Original space with PCA arrows
plot(df_s[, 1], df_s[, 2], pch = 19, col = "gray40", asp = 1,
  main = "Original Space + PCA Directions",
  xlab = "Feature 1 (standardized)", ylab = "Feature 2 (standardized)")

# PC1 direction
arrows(0, 0, pca$rotation[1, 1] * 2, pca$rotation[2, 1] * 2,
  col = "coral", lwd = 3, length = 0.15)
text(pca$rotation[1, 1] * 2.3, pca$rotation[2, 1] * 2.3,
  "PC1", col = "coral", font = 2, cex = 1.2)

# PC2 direction
arrows(0, 0, pca$rotation[1, 2] * 1.5, pca$rotation[2, 2] * 1.5,
  col = "steelblue", lwd = 3, length = 0.15)
text(pca$rotation[1, 2] * 1.8, pca$rotation[2, 2] * 1.8,
  "PC2", col = "steelblue", font = 2, cex = 1.2)

# Rotated space (PCA scores)
scores <- pca$x
plot(scores[, 1], scores[, 2], pch = 19, col = "gray40", asp = 1,
  main = "PCA Space (Rotated)",
  xlab = "PC1 (most variance)", ylab = "PC2 (remaining variance)")
abline(h = 0, v = 0, lty = 2, col = "gray70")

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

The eigenvalues and the share of variance each component captures.

```{r}
#| label: plot-eigenvalues
#| fig-cap: "Eigenvalues tell you how much variance each component captures"

# Show eigenvalues
eigenvalues <- pca$sdev^2
var_explained <- eigenvalues / sum(eigenvalues) * 100

cat("Eigenvalues:\n")
cat(sprintf("  PC1: %.2f (%.1f%% of variance)\n", eigenvalues[1], var_explained[1]))
cat(sprintf("  PC2: %.2f (%.1f%% of variance)\n", eigenvalues[2], var_explained[2]))
cat(sprintf("\nPC1 alone captures %.1f%% of the information!\n", var_explained[1]))
cat("With correlated data, you can often drop PC2 and lose very little.")
```

Ten correlated features, all driven by two hidden factors, and how the variance piles up in the first few components.

```{r}
#| label: plot-high-dim
#| fig-cap: "10 correlated features compressed into components — most variance in first 2-3"

set.seed(42)

# Generate 10 correlated features (all driven by 2 hidden factors)
hidden1 <- rnorm(n)
hidden2 <- rnorm(n)

features <- matrix(nrow = n, ncol = 10)
for (j in 1:10) {
  w1 <- runif(1, 0.5, 1.5) * sample(c(-1, 1), 1)
  w2 <- runif(1, 0.2, 0.8) * sample(c(-1, 1), 1)
  features[, j] <- w1 * hidden1 + w2 * hidden2 + rnorm(n, 0, 0.5)
}
colnames(features) <- paste0("X", 1:10)

# PCA
pca10 <- prcomp(scale(features))
var_exp10 <- pca10$sdev^2 / sum(pca10$sdev^2) * 100
cum_var <- cumsum(var_exp10)

par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))

# Scree plot
barplot(var_exp10, names.arg = paste0("PC", 1:10),
  col = ifelse(cum_var <= 90, "steelblue", "gray80"),
  main = "Scree Plot: Variance per Component",
  ylab = "% Variance Explained", las = 2)

# Cumulative variance
plot(1:10, cum_var, type = "b", pch = 19, col = "steelblue", lwd = 2,
  main = "Cumulative Variance Explained",
  xlab = "Number of Components", ylab = "% Total Variance",
  ylim = c(0, 100))
abline(h = 90, lty = 2, col = "coral")
text(7, 85, "90% threshold", col = "coral", cex = 0.9)

# Mark how many needed for 90%
n_for_90 <- which(cum_var >= 90)[1]
points(n_for_90, cum_var[n_for_90], pch = 19, cex = 2, col = "coral")
text(n_for_90 + 1, cum_var[n_for_90] - 5,
  paste0(n_for_90, " components\nfor 90%"), col = "coral", cex = 0.9)

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

**10 features → `r n_for_90` components** that capture 90%+ of the information. The remaining components are mostly noise.

The scree plot for the same ten features. Look for the elbow.

```{r}
#| label: plot-scree-elbow
#| fig-cap: "The scree plot elbow suggests 2-3 components are sufficient"

plot(1:10, pca10$sdev^2, type = "b", pch = 19, col = "steelblue", lwd = 2,
  main = "Scree Plot: Look for the Elbow",
  xlab = "Component Number", ylab = "Eigenvalue")

# Highlight the elbow
points(3, pca10$sdev[3]^2, pch = 1, cex = 3, col = "coral", lwd = 2)
text(4.5, pca10$sdev[3]^2, "Elbow here →\nkeep 2-3 components",
  col = "coral", cex = 0.9)
```

The trap: data built so that the signal sits in a low-variance direction.

```{r}
#| label: plot-pca-trap
#| fig-cap: "PC1 has the most variance but PC3 actually predicts the response"

set.seed(42)

# Create data where the signal is in a low-variance direction
n_trap <- 150
noise_big <- rnorm(n_trap, 0, 5)    # big variance, no signal
noise_med <- rnorm(n_trap, 0, 3)    # medium variance, no signal
signal <- rnorm(n_trap, 0, 1)       # small variance, IS the signal

X_trap <- cbind(
  noise_big + 0.1 * signal,
  noise_med + 0.05 * signal,
  0.5 * noise_big + 0.8 * signal    # signal mixed in
)

y_trap <- 3 * signal + rnorm(n_trap, 0, 0.5)  # y depends on the hidden signal

pca_trap <- prcomp(scale(X_trap))

# Correlation of each PC with y
pc_cor <- sapply(1:3, function(j) cor(pca_trap$x[, j], y_trap))

par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))

barplot(pca_trap$sdev^2, names.arg = paste0("PC", 1:3),
  col = "steelblue", main = "Variance (what PCA ranks by)",
  ylab = "Eigenvalue")

barplot(abs(pc_cor), names.arg = paste0("PC", 1:3),
  col = c("gray70", "gray70", "coral"),
  main = "Correlation with Y (what matters!)",
  ylab = "|Correlation with response|")

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

cat("PC1 has the MOST variance but the LEAST predictive power.\n")
cat("PC3 has the LEAST variance but the MOST predictive power.\n")
cat("\nThis is why you MUST validate PCA-based models on actual prediction.\n")
cat("Don't blindly drop low-variance components!")
```

Why you standardise first. Without scaling, the feature with the larger range dominates PC1.

```{r}
#| label: plot-scaling-pca
#| fig-cap: "Without scaling, the high-range feature dominates PC1"

set.seed(42)

# Income: 30k-90k, Age: 20-65
data_unscaled <- data.frame(
  income = rnorm(80, 60000, 15000),
  age = rnorm(80, 40, 10)
)

pca_unscaled <- prcomp(data_unscaled, scale. = FALSE)
pca_scaled <- prcomp(data_unscaled, scale. = TRUE)

par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))

# Loadings comparison
barplot(abs(pca_unscaled$rotation[, 1]), names.arg = c("Income", "Age"),
  col = c("coral", "steelblue"), main = "PC1 Loadings: UNSCALED",
  ylab = "Absolute Loading")
mtext("Income dominates (larger range)", side = 1, line = 2.5, cex = 0.8, col = "red")

barplot(abs(pca_scaled$rotation[, 1]), names.arg = c("Income", "Age"),
  col = c("coral", "steelblue"), main = "PC1 Loadings: SCALED",
  ylab = "Absolute Loading")
mtext("Both contribute fairly", side = 1, line = 2.5, cex = 0.8, col = "darkgreen")

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

Heteroscedasticity: the spread of the response grows with x, and the residual plot shows a funnel.

```{r}
#| label: plot-heteroscedasticity
#| fig-cap: "The funnel shape: variance increases with the predicted value"

set.seed(42)
x_bc <- runif(100, 1, 20)
y_bc <- 2 * x_bc + rnorm(100, 0, x_bc * 0.8)  # variance grows with x

df_bc <- data.frame(x = x_bc, y = y_bc)
fit_bc <- lm(y ~ x, data = df_bc)

par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))

plot(df_bc$x, df_bc$y, pch = 19, col = "gray40",
  main = "Data: Variance Grows with X",
  xlab = "X", ylab = "Y")
abline(fit_bc, col = "steelblue", lwd = 2)

plot(fitted(fit_bc), residuals(fit_bc), pch = 19, col = "gray40",
  main = "Residual Plot: Funnel Shape",
  xlab = "Fitted Values", ylab = "Residuals")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2, col = "coral")
text(25, 15, "Variance increases →\n(heteroscedasticity)", col = "coral", cex = 0.9)

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

The Box-Cox profile from `MASS::boxcox`, and the optimal $\lambda$ it finds.

```{r}
#| label: plot-boxcox-lambda
#| fig-cap: "Box-Cox finds the optimal λ that stabilizes variance"

library(MASS)

# Need positive y for Box-Cox
y_pos <- y_bc - min(y_bc) + 1
df_pos <- data.frame(x = x_bc, y = y_pos)
fit_pos <- lm(y ~ x, data = df_pos)

# Box-Cox profile
bc <- boxcox(fit_pos, plotit = TRUE)

# Find optimal lambda
optimal_lambda <- bc$x[which.max(bc$y)]
cat(sprintf("\nOptimal λ = %.2f\n", optimal_lambda))
cat(sprintf("Closest standard transform: %s\n",
  ifelse(abs(optimal_lambda) < 0.2, "log(y)",
    ifelse(abs(optimal_lambda - 0.5) < 0.2, "√y",
      ifelse(abs(optimal_lambda - 1) < 0.2, "no transform needed",
        paste0("y^", round(optimal_lambda, 2)))))))
```

Residuals before and after the transform.

```{r}
#| label: plot-boxcox-effect
#| fig-cap: "Before and after Box-Cox: the funnel shape disappears"

# Apply transform
if (abs(optimal_lambda) < 0.01) {
  y_transformed <- log(y_pos)
} else {
  y_transformed <- (y_pos^optimal_lambda - 1) / optimal_lambda
}

df_trans <- data.frame(x = x_bc, y = y_transformed)
fit_trans <- lm(y ~ x, data = df_trans)

par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))

# Before
plot(fitted(fit_pos), residuals(fit_pos), pch = 19, col = "coral",
  main = "BEFORE Box-Cox: Residuals",
  xlab = "Fitted", ylab = "Residual")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)

hist(residuals(fit_pos), breaks = 15, col = "coral", border = "white",
  main = "BEFORE: Residual Distribution", xlab = "Residual")

# After
plot(fitted(fit_trans), residuals(fit_trans), pch = 19, col = "steelblue",
  main = "AFTER Box-Cox: Residuals",
  xlab = "Fitted", ylab = "Residual")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)

hist(residuals(fit_trans), breaks = 15, col = "steelblue", border = "white",
  main = "AFTER: Residual Distribution", xlab = "Residual")

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

Two unrelated series that both trend upward, before and after detrending.

```{r}
#| label: plot-detrending
#| fig-cap: "Both variables trend upward with time → spurious correlation. Detrending reveals the truth."

set.seed(42)
time_dt <- 1:60

# Two UNRELATED things that both trend upward
ice_cream <- 10 + 0.3 * time_dt + rnorm(60, 0, 2)
drownings <- 5 + 0.15 * time_dt + rnorm(60, 0, 1.5)

par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))

# Raw correlation (spurious)
plot(ice_cream, drownings, pch = 19, col = "coral",
  main = paste0("Raw: r = ", round(cor(ice_cream, drownings), 2)),
  xlab = "Ice Cream Sales", ylab = "Drownings")
abline(lm(drownings ~ ice_cream), col = "coral", lwd = 2)

# Both trending
plot(time_dt, ice_cream, type = "l", col = "coral", lwd = 2,
  main = "Both variables trend with time",
  xlab = "Time", ylab = "Value", ylim = c(0, 35))
lines(time_dt, drownings, col = "steelblue", lwd = 2)
legend("topleft", legend = c("Ice cream", "Drownings"), bty = "n",
  col = c("coral", "steelblue"), lwd = 2, cex = 0.8)

# Detrend
ice_dt <- residuals(lm(ice_cream ~ time_dt))
drown_dt <- residuals(lm(drownings ~ time_dt))

# Detrended correlation (real)
plot(ice_dt, drown_dt, pch = 19, col = "steelblue",
  main = paste0("Detrended: r = ", round(cor(ice_dt, drown_dt), 2)),
  xlab = "Ice Cream (detrended)", ylab = "Drownings (detrended)")
abline(lm(drown_dt ~ ice_dt), col = "steelblue", lwd = 2)

# Detrended series
plot(time_dt, ice_dt, type = "l", col = "coral", lwd = 2,
  main = "After detrending: no trend",
  xlab = "Time", ylab = "Detrended Value")
lines(time_dt, drown_dt, col = "steelblue", lwd = 2)
abline(h = 0, lty = 2, col = "gray50")

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

PCA followed by regression: three components against all ten predictors.

```{r}
#| label: plot-pca-regression
#| fig-cap: "PCA + regression: compress 10 features into 3 components, then regress"

# Use the 10-feature data from earlier
y_demo <- 2 * hidden1 - 1.5 * hidden2 + rnorm(n, 0, 0.5)

# Full regression (all 10 features)
fit_full <- lm(y_demo ~ features)

# PCA regression (3 components)
scores3 <- pca10$x[, 1:3]
fit_pca <- lm(y_demo ~ scores3)

cat("=== Full model (10 predictors) ===\n")
cat(sprintf("  R² = %.3f\n", summary(fit_full)$r.squared))
cat(sprintf("  Adj R² = %.3f\n\n", summary(fit_full)$adj.r.squared))

cat("=== PCA model (3 components) ===\n")
cat(sprintf("  R² = %.3f\n", summary(fit_pca)$r.squared))
cat(sprintf("  Adj R² = %.3f\n", summary(fit_pca)$adj.r.squared))
cat("\n10 predictors → 3 components with similar Adj R²")
cat("\nSimpler model, less overfitting risk, no multicollinearity")
```
:::
